content: The pneumococcal vaccine is designed to protect against infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. For example, the conjugate vaccine (e.g., Prevnar) has been recommended since 2000 for all children aged 2–23 months and for at-risk children aged 24–59 months. The standard vaccination schedule involves a four-dose series administered at 2, 4, 6, and 12–14 months of age. This vaccine provides effective protection against severe pneumococcal infections, particularly septicemia and meningitis. However, if a child is exposed to a pneumococcal serotype not included in the vaccine, they will not be protected. This limitation, along with the potential for conjugate vaccines to promote the spread of non-covered serotypes, has driven research into vaccines that could provide broader, species-wide protection. The pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (e.g., Pneumovax) offers at least 85% protection in individuals under 55 years of age for a duration of five years or longer. Immunization is particularly recommended for those at the highest risk of infection, including individuals aged 65 years or older. Generally, this vaccine is administered as a single lifetime dose due to the increased risk of adverse effects with repeated doses. However, revaccination may be indicated for individuals with specific conditions, such as asplenia or nephrotic syndrome. The standard 23-valent polysaccharide vaccines are ineffective in children under two years of age. Current guidelines from the American College of Physicians recommend vaccination between the ages of 2 and 65 when indicated, or at age 65. If someone received the vaccine before age 60, a one-time revaccination is advised. In the UK, it was announced in February 2006 that the government would introduce the conjugate vaccine for children at 2, 4, and 13 months of age, starting on September 4, 2006. This change was part of broader updates to the immunization program. In 2009, the European Medicines Agency approved the use of a 10-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine for use in Europe. Globally, the Pneumococcal Vaccines Accelerated Development and Introduction Plan (PneumoADIP) aims to expedite the evaluation and accessibility of new pneumococcal vaccines in developing countries. This initiative is funded by the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization (GAVI). By 2010, 30 GAVI countries had expressed interest in participating, with the goal of vaccinating 4 million children by 2030. Research into pneumococcal vaccines continues, particularly to address the geographic variability of pneumococcal serotypes and to develop the most effective vaccines for populations in developing countries. Studies have identified the most common pneumococcal serotypes in developed countries as 14, 6, 19, 18, 9, 23, 7, 4, 1, and 15, while in developing countries, the order is 6, 14, 8, 5, 1, 19, 9, 23, 18, 15, and 7. Advanced Market Commitments represent a novel approach to public health funding, designed to stimulate the development and production of vaccines for use in developing countries. There is ongoing research into alternative methods of vaccine delivery, such as intranasal administration, which may enhance vaccine efficacy and eliminate the need for injections. Additionally, the development of serotype-specific anticapsular monoclonal antibodies has shown promise in preclinical studies. These antibodies have been demonstrated to prolong survival in mouse models of pneumococcal infection by reducing bacterial loads and suppressing the host inflammatory response. Efforts are also underway to develop vaccines that provide broad protection against pneumococcal disease.
